cr.tip.missWin: 💡 Before each move, look for a chain of bridges that already reaches both of your edges.
cr.tip.allowWin: 💡 Check the opponent's shortest connection: if it needs only one more stone, block it first.
cr.tip.bridge: 💡 A bridge has two empty cells; when the opponent takes one, take the other at once.
cr.tip.swap: 💡 With the swap rule, strong first moves (near the centre) should be swapped; weak ones (on the border) should not.
cr.tip.edge: 💡 Stones on the board's border reach few cells. In the opening, play nearer the centre or use edge templates (the 2nd and 3rd rows).
cr.tip.gen: 💡 On the board, the numbers are the winning chances of the best cells.
rl.title: Learn the rules
intro.hist: Hex was invented by the Danish poet and mathematician Piet Hein in 1942 and, independently, by John Nash at Princeton in 1948. Mathematicians played it on bathroom tiles; it was sold as "Hex" by Parker Brothers in 1952.
intro.win: Players take turns placing a stone on any empty hexagon. Red joins its two red edges, Blue its two blue edges with an unbroken chain. Stones never move or get captured, and there are no draws.
intro.cult: Nash proved that the first player always has a winning strategy — without saying what it is. That is why the swap rule is used: Blue may take over Red's first stone. Hex is a classic of AI research (programs such as MoHex) and of combinatorial game theory.
tr.board.b: Hex is played on a rhombus of hexagons. Each player owns two opposite edges. Red (first) wants to join the two red edges, Blue the two blue edges. The corner cells belong to both.
tr.place.b: On your turn, put one stone on any empty cell. Stones are never moved or captured.
tr.place.task: Place a red stone on any empty cell.
tr.place.ok: That's it! The stones stay where they are until the end.
tr.goal.b: Stones on touching hexagons are connected. When your stones form a chain from one of your edges to the other, you win.
tr.goal.task: Finish the red chain from edge to edge.
tr.goal.ng: Look for the one cell that closes the gap in the red chain.
tr.block.b: Your stone also blocks: the opponent's chain cannot pass through it. Here Blue is one stone away from connecting.
tr.block.ok: Blocked! Blue must find another way round.
tr.block.ng: Blue can still connect with one stone. Put your stone on that cell.
tr.bridge.b: Two stones with two empty cells between them form a bridge: if the opponent takes one cell, you take the other and stay connected. Blue has just intruded into your bridge.
tr.bridge.task: Answer the intrusion and keep your chain connected.
tr.bridge.ok: Saved — and the chain reaches both edges!
tr.bridge.ng: Take the other cell of the bridge.
tr.nodraw.b: When the board is full, exactly one player has a chain: to block your opponent completely, you must connect yourself. So every game of Hex has a winner.
tr.swap.b: The first player has a big advantage. With the swap rule, Blue may answer Red's first move by swapping: the stone becomes Blue's (mirrored across the board's long diagonal) and Red moves again.
tr.swap.task: You are Blue. Press "Swap" to take over Red's strong first stone.
tr.swap.ok: Swapped! The stone is Blue's now — so Red should open with a move that is not too strong.
tr.swap.hint: Press the "Swap" button above the board.
rt.title: Your rating
rt.desc: Rated games are played on 11×11 with the swap rule. Opponents (AI from 15 kyu to 5 dan) are chosen to match your rating (starting at 1000). Usually they are close to your level, sometimes stronger or weaker. Win to go up, lose to go down. Your side is random, there are no hints, and you have 5 minutes plus 3 seconds per move.
rt.noEval: No evaluation during a rated game
rt.abandonQ: A rated game is in progress. Leaving now abandons it and counts as a loss. Continue?
ls.title: Lessons
ls.desc: "Hex for beginners" starts from connecting and blocking; "Tactics" teaches bridges, ladders and edge templates; "Strategy" is about the opening and the swap rule. Each step has 5 problems (20 points each, 75 to pass), all checked by the engine.
course.basics.sub: Start here once you know the rules: connecting, blocking, the bridge and the edge — checked with problems.
course.tactics.sub: Bridges, ladders, ladder escapes and edge templates: the patterns strong players see at a glance.
course.strategy.sub: Blocking at a distance, the centre, and how to use the swap rule — judged by the AI's winning chances.
course.graduate: 🎉 "Hex for beginners" completed! You are ready to play — try the AI at 15 kyu to 10 kyu on 7×7 or 9×9 first.
op.title: Openings
op.desc: The first-move map shows the AI's winning chances for Red after every first move (which openings to swap). The studies replay typical lines played by the engine with notes; then practise the key moves.
op.credit: All lines, maps and values were computed by this site's AI (MCTS). Opening names follow common Hex usage (e.g. "a3 opening").

op.practiceDesc: 5 problems from this opening. The best move scores 20; close moves score by how little they lose

op.studyEnd: That is the main line. Go on to "Practice".

fm.title: First-move map {n}×{n}
fm.desc: Every cell shows Red's winning chance (%) when Red opens there and Blue does not swap. Red cells are good for Red — swap them; blue cells are good for Blue.
fm.how: Each first move was searched by the AI with Blue to reply (swap off). Red cells (above 50%) are worth swapping; with the swap rule, Red should open on a cell close to 50%.
fm.fair: Close to 50% (good openings with the swap rule): {list}
fm.note: AI search of about {s} s per cell. In theory Red wins after most first moves on boards up to 9×9; the percentages show how hard it is in practice.
pz.title: Hex puzzles
pz.desc: "Connect in N": join your edges within N moves whatever the opponent does. "Stop": find the only move that prevents the opponent's forced connection. Every puzzle was checked by the engine's solver: one correct first move.
pz.start: Play the move that leads to a connection.
pz.startBlock: Find the one move that stops the connection.
pz.good: Good move. Waiting for the reply…
pz.solvedBlock: No forced connection within {k} moves any more.
pz.hintText: The dashed rings mark the area where the connection is made.
pz.hintBlock: The dashed rings mark the area of the threat.
pz.answerDoneBlock: That is the only move that stops the connection.
pz.stray: You left the solution. The opponent answers with its best move.

pz.goalBlock: {c} to move: stop {o} from connecting within {k} moves
